<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#A2.SS3" title="In Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">B.3 </span>Accuracy reported for BERT on GLUE</span></a></li>
</ol></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_appendix"><a href="#A3" title="In ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">C </span>PTQ challenge of BERT<math class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{{base}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{{base}}}</annotation></semantics></math></span></a></li>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Zhewei Yao
</span><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_note_frontmatter ltx_thanks_note ltx_role_thanks"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">thanks: </span>Code will be released soon as a part of <a href="https://github.com/microsoft/DeepSpeed" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/microsoft/DeepSpeed</a></span></span></span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Xiaoxia Wu, Conglong Li, Yuxiong He 
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Reza Yazdani Aminabadi
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Microsoft
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Minjia Zhang
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span><span id="id2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">{zheweiyao, yazdani.reza, minjiaz, xiaoxiawu, conglong.li, yuxhe}@microsoft.com</span>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">How to efficiently serve ever-larger trained natural language models in practice has become exceptionally challenging even for powerful cloud servers due to their prohibitive memory/computation requirements.
In this work, we present an efficient and affordable post-training quantization approach to compress large Transformer-based models, termed as ZeroQuant.
ZeroQuant is an end-to-end quantization and inference pipeline with three main components:
(1) a fine-grained hardware-friendly quantization scheme for both weight and activations;
(2) a novel affordable layer-by-layer knowledge distillation algorithm (LKD) even without the access to the original training data;
(3) a highly-optimized quantization system backend support to remove the quantization/dequantization overhead.
As such, we are able to show that:
(1) ZeroQuant can reduce the precision for weights and activations to INT8 in a cost-free way for both BERT and GPT-3-style models with minimal accuracy impact, which leads to up to 5.19x/4.16x speedup on those models compared to FP16 inference;
(2) ZeroQuant plus LKD affordably quantize the weights in the fully-connected module to INT4 along with INT8 weights in the attention module and INT8 activations, resulting in 3x memory footprint reduction compared to the FP16 model;
(3) ZeroQuant can be directly applied to two of the largest open-sourced language models, including GPT-J<math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{6B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>6B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{6B}}</annotation></semantics></math> and GPT-NeoX<math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{20B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>20B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{20B}}</annotation></semantics></math>, for which our INT8 model achieves similar accuracy as the FP16 model but achieves up to 5.2x better efficiency.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large-scale natural language models have been widely adopted in different applications, e.g., natural language understanding using BERT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>]</cite> and generation tasks using GPT-style models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>]</cite>.
Although those models have achieved cutting-edge accuracy results, as the model size keeps increasing dramatically, the requirements of memory footprint and the computational cost to deploy them become a major bottleneck, even on cloud servers with powerful GPU devices.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">One promising way to alleviate this challenge is quantization, which can reduce the bit precision for both weight and activations for lower memory footprint and faster compute (e.g., INT8 Tensor cores on T4/A100).
However, quantization usually requires retraining (also known as quantization aware training, or QAT in short) to recover the accuracy degradation from representation loss of weight and activations.
To enable QAT, the full training pipeline is usually required, including the training data and compute resources, to finetune the model.
Access to those components is now oftentimes not available, and QAT is also a time-consuming process, particularly for those large-scale models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Recently, zero-shot quantization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>]</cite> and post-training quantization (PTQ) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>, <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> are proposed to address the training-data access and compute requirement challenges since PTQ generally requires no (or minimal) retraining.
But most of those works primarily focus on computer vision problems on relatively small scales.
More recently, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite> shows promising PTQ results on BERT.
However, (1) its main focus is on high-precision quantization (INT8/FP16) on BERT<math id="S1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{{base}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{{base}}}</annotation></semantics></math>, (2) it does not consider other billion-scale generative models (GPT-3-style models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>). More importantly, most of these works do not report real latency improvement, putting the usefulness of these methods in improving inference latency into question.
For example, existing work often do not discuss the quantization/dequantization cost associated with different quantization schemes, which in fact has a big impact to the performance benefit of using low precision.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Besides, for extreme quantization (e.g., INT4), knowledge distillation is usually used to boost performance, which adds another source of expensive computation cost as compared to QAT.
Furthermore, in order to achieve better accuracy performance, hidden-states knowledge distillation, e.g., <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">79</a>]</cite>, is usually applied for the quantized model.
This would put significant pressure on the GPU memory and the compute resource requirement since both the teacher and student models needed to be loaded into the GPU memory for training.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we present ZeroQuant, an end-to-end post-training quantization and inference pipeline, to address those challenges, targeting both INT8 and INT4/INT8 mixed-precision quantization.
Specifically, our contributions are:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We apply fine-grained hardware-friendly quantization schemes on both weight and activations, i.e., group-wise quantization for weight and token-wise quantization for activations.
Both quantization schemes can significantly reduce the quantization error and retain hardware acceleration properties.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose a novel layer-by-layer knowledge distillation method (LKD) for INT4/INT8 mixed-precision quantization, where the neural network is quantized layer-by-layer through distillation with minimal iterations and even without the access to the original training data.
As such, at any given moment, the device memory is primarily populated only with a single extra layer’s footprint, making billion-scale model distillation feasible with limited training budget and GPU devices.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We develop a highly optimized inference backend, which eliminates the expensive computation cost of quantization/dequantization operators, enabling latency speedups on INT8 Tensor cores on modern GPU hardware.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our empirical results show that:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1.i4.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">–</span></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">ZeroQuant enables quantizing BERT and GPT-3-style models into INT8 weight and activations to retain accuracy without incurring any retraining cost.
Compared to FP16 inference, our INT8 model achieves up to 5.19x/4.16x speedup on BERT<math id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{{base}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{{base}}}</annotation></semantics></math>/GPT-3<math id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{350M}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>350M</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{350M}}</annotation></semantics></math> on A100 GPUs.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">–</span></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">ZeroQuant plus LKD can do INT4/INT8 mixed-precision quantization for BERT and GPT-3-style models.
This results in a 3x memory footprint reduction with marginal accuracy loss as compared to the FP16 model.
Also, thanks to the lightweight of LKD,
we can finish the quantization process in 33s (10 minutes) for BERT<math id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{{base}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{{base}}}</annotation></semantics></math> (BERT<math id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{large}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>large</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{large}}</annotation></semantics></math>).
We also demonstrate that LKD can use other datasets to achieve similar performance to the original training data.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">–</span></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We demonstrate the scalability of ZeroQuant on two of the largest open-sourced language models, i.e, GPT-J<math id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{6B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>6B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{6B}}</annotation></semantics></math> and GPT-NeoX<math id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{20B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>20B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{20B}}</annotation></semantics></math>, with INT8 quantization.
ZeroQuant can achieve 3.67x speedup over the FP16 model for GPT-J<math id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{6B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>6B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{6B}}</annotation></semantics></math> and (2) reduce the GPU requirement for inference from 2 to 1 and latency from 65ms to 25ms for GPT-NeoX<math id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{20B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>20B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{20B}}</annotation></semantics></math> (i.e., 5.2x better system efficiency in total).</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Model compression has been explored from different aspects <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>, <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">74</a>, <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">55</a>, <a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>, <a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">60</a>, <a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">68</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite>.
Among those, quantization is one of the most promising directions as it directly reduces the memory footprint and compute intensity.
Here, we focus on quantization for NLP models and briefly discuss the related work.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The majority of quantization works can be categorized into quantization-aware training (QAT).
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>, <a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">76</a>]</cite> are the first few works to quantize BERT models using integer numbers for both weight and activations.
Particularly, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>]</cite> utilizes Hessian information to push the weight bit-precision to even INT2/INT4, and it also proposes group-wise quantization to quantize the weight matrix in a more fine-grained granularity compared to single matrix quantization.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite> introduces quantization noise to alleviate the variations of QAT.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">79</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite> leverage very expensive knowledge distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite> and data augmentation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite> to ternarize/binarize weights.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite> combines knowledge distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite> and learned step size quantization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite> to quantize the weight to 2–8 bits.
Recently, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>]</cite> also uses knowledge distillation to compress GPT-2 models on task-specific problems to INT2.
All those works quantize models using the original training datasets.
More importantly they need retraining or finetuning the full model to recover the accuracy, and such compute cost on extra-large models, like  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>, can be hardly affordable for most research labs or practitioners.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">One solution to overcome the compute cost challenge is post-training quantization (PTQ). However, PTQ often induces a significant drop in accuracy because the network can be sensitive to quantization errors.
Along this line, one of the first works applied to Transformer-based <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">64</a>]</cite> models is <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">75</a>]</cite>.
The authors introduce centroid-based quantization method, where outlier numbers use FP32 format and the rest numbers are quantized using non-uniform quantization.
As such, it is hard to get the real inference latency benefit on general compute accelerators, e.g., CPU and GPU, because the parallel processing units in these hardware do not support efficient computation of mixed data types.
More recently, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite> introduces high-precision activation quantization (FP16) for part of the model to overcome the high dynamic activation ranges.
However, to the best of our knowledge,
(1) How to apply PTQ on GPT-3-style models while achieving high accuracy has not been studied in any of previous work yet;
(2) How to apply PTQ on billion (or even a dozen of billions) scale model is still under-explored;
(3) Efficient inference system backend is still missing, especially for fine-grained quantization schemes, making it hard to achieve low latency on commodity hardware.
ZeroQuant resolves all those limitations by considering the system backend into the algorithm design and we verify its capability on both BERT and large-scale GPT-3-style (up to 20 billion, i.e., GPT-NeoX<math id="S2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{20B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>20B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{20B}}</annotation></semantics></math>) models for various tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Background and Challenge</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We give a brief overview of the transformer architecture and quantization background in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Background ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.
Please refer to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">64</a>]</cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite> for more details about the transformer architecture and quantization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Post-training quantization (PTQ) exhibits great compression efficiency compared to quantization-aware training (QAT) since PTQ is usually applied to quantize the model without retraining.
A common strategy of PTQ is to feed the training data to the network and calibrate the scaling factor, <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>, using the running mean.
Please see Appendix <a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Details of PTQ on BERT and GPT ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a> for more details.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Some work has been done for BERT<math id="S3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{{base}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{{base}}}</annotation></semantics></math> models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite> with INT8 weight and mixed INT8/FP16 activation quantization.
However, there is no investigation for (1) even lower bit-precision PTQ on BERT models and (2) large-scale GPT-3-style models.
Here, we briefly discuss the challenge of the application of PTQ on both BERT (in Appendix <a href="#A3" title='Appendix C PTQ challenge of BERT_"base" ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers' class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>) and GPT-3-style models.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2206.01861v1/gpt_activation_range_analysis.svg" id="S3.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:215/156;" width="215" height="156"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2206.01861v1/gpt_weight_range_analysis.svg" id="S3.F1.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:215/155;" width="215" height="155"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>
The activation range (left) and row-wise weight range of the attention output matrix (right) of different layers on the pretrained GPT-3<math id="S3.F1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{350M}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>350M</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{350M}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
See Figure <a href="#A3.F1" title='Figure C.1 ‣ Appendix C PTQ challenge of BERT_"base" ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers' class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1</span></a> for the results of BERT<math id="S3.F1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{{base}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{{base}}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The results of GPT-3<math id="S3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{350M}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>350M</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{350M}}</annotation></semantics></math> with PTQ are shown in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3 Background and Challenge ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
As can be seen, the INT8 activation quantization (i.e., the row of W16A8) causes the primary accuracy loss.
Further pushing the weight to INT8 (i.e., the row of W8A8) does not change the accuracy of zero-shot evaluation tasks but leads the causal language modeling task (Wikitext-2) to worse perplexity score,
which demonstrates the sensitivity of generation tasks as compared to other zero-shot evaluation problems.
For W4/8A16, on some accuracy-based tasks, GPT-3<math id="S3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{350M}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>350M</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{350M}}</annotation></semantics></math> still achieves reasonable performance like OpenBookQA but it loses accuracy on the majority of the rest tasks.
Particularly, for Wikitext-2, GPT-3<math id="S3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{350M}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>350M</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{350M}}</annotation></semantics></math> with W4/8A16 cannot generate any meaningful text anymore.
Please also see Appendix <a href="#A3" title='Appendix C PTQ challenge of BERT_"base" ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers' class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> for the analysis for BERT.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>
Post training quantization results of GPT-3<math id="S3.T1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{350M}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>350M</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{350M}}</annotation></semantics></math> on 20 zero-shot evaluation datesets.
Here WxAy means x-/y-bit for weight/activation.
Particularly, for W4/8, we quantize the MHSA’s weight to INT8 and FFC’s weight to INT4.

</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dynamic Activation Range</span>
To investigate why INT8 activation leads to significant accuracy drop for both BERT and GPT-3-style models, we plot the token-wise (i.e., the hidden state of each token) range of each activation for different transformer layers of GPT-3<math id="S3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{350M}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>350M</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{350M}}</annotation></semantics></math> in Figure <a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 3 Background and Challenge ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> (left).
As can be seen, different tokens have dramatically different activation ranges.
For example, the maximum range of the last layer is around 35 but the minimum range is close to 8. This larger variance in the activation range makes it difficult to use a fixed quantization range (usually the maximum value) for all tokens to retain the prediction accuracy, because the limited representation power for small range tokens is going to hurt the accuracy performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Different Ranges of Neurons in Weight Matrices</span>
Similarly, we plot the row-wise (i.e., the output dimension) weight range of the attention output matrix (<math id="S3.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bm{W}}_{o}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝑾</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{W}}_{o}</annotation></semantics></math>) of GPT-3<math id="S3.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{350M}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>350M</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{350M}}</annotation></semantics></math> in Figure <a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 3 Background and Challenge ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> (right).
There is a 10x difference between the largest magnitudes of different rows and this leads to the worse generation performance of the INT8 weight PTQ.
This also makes it very challenging when INT4 quantization is applied as the INT4 only has 16 numbers and a 10x smaller range leads to 2 (or 3) numbers for the representations of those smaller-range rows.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">This analysis results also indicate why more expensive hidden-states knowledge distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite> is used for ultra-low precision quantization to close the accuracy gap.
However, as the training cost of knowledge distillation for large-scale models is too high, a lightweight and efficient method is desirable for PTQ.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Methodology</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Fine-grained Hardware-friendly Quantization Scheme</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Background and Challenge ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, even applying INT8 PTQ to BERT/GPT-3-style models leads to significant accuracy degradation.
The key challenge is the representation of INT8 cannot fully capture the different numerical ranges of different rows in weight matrices and different activation tokens.
One way to address this is to use group-wise (token-wise) quantization for the weight matrix (activations).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Group-wise Quantization for Weights</span> Group-wise weight matrix quantization has first been proposed in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>]</cite>,
where a weight matrix <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n\times m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n\times m}</annotation></semantics></math> is partitioned in to <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> groups, and each group is quantized separately.
However, in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>]</cite>, the authors only apply this for quantization aware training.
More importantly, they do not consider the hardware efficiency constraint and they do not have a system backend support.
As such, they lack the real latency reduction benefit.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In our design, we consider the hardware constraint from Ampere Architecture of GPUs (e.g, A100), where the compute unit is based on Warp Matrix Multiply and Accumulate (WMMA) tiling size <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite> to achieve the best speedup.
Later, we will show that our group-wise quantization leads to much better accuracy as compared to single-matrix quantization due to its finer-granularity quantization while still achieving great latency reduction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Token-wise Quantization for Activations</span>
As mentioned in Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Background and Challenge ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2" title="A.2 Quantization Background ‣ Appendix A Background ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a>, a common practice for existing PTQ work is to use static quantization for activation, where the min/max range is calculated at an offline calibration phase.
Such a method might be sufficient for small scale models where the variance in the activation range is small.
However, as analyzed in Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Background and Challenge ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, there is a huge variance in the activation range for large-scale transformer models such as GPT-3<math id="S4.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{350M}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>350M</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{350M}}</annotation></semantics></math> and BERT<math id="S4.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{{base}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{{base}}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
As such, a static quantization scheme (often applied to all tokens/samples) would lead to significant accuracy drop.
One natural idea to overcome this issue is to adopt finer-grained token-wise quantization and dynamically calculate the min/max range for each token to reduce the quantization error from activations.
Our evaluation in  Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Results ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> also shows that token-wise quantization for activation significantly improves the accuracy of GPT-3-style and BERT models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">However, directly applying token-wise quantization using existing DL frameworks, such as the PyTorch quantization suite, would lead to significant quantization and dequantization cost because token-wise quantization introduces additional operations that lead to expensive data movement overhead between the GPU compute units and the main memory.
To address this issue, we build a highly optimized inference backend for token-wise quantization of transformer models. For example, the inference backend of ZeroQuant employs so called <em id="S4.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">kernel fusion</em> technique to fuse quantization operator with its previous operator, like layer normalization, to alleviate the data movement cost from token-wise quantization. Similarly, the dequantization cost of the different GeMMs’ output is alleviated by scaling the INT32 accumulation using both
the weight and activation quantization scales, before writing the final FP16 result back to the main memory for the next FP16 operator (like GeLU).
Those optimization will be discussed in more details in Section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Quantization-Optimized Transformer Kernels ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Token-wise quantization can significantly reduce the representation error for quantized activations.
Also, as it does not need to calibrate the activation range, later we will show that there is no quantization-related cost (e.g., activation range calibration) for a moderate quantization scheme (INT8 weight with INT8 activation) for ZeroQuant.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Layer-by-layer Knowledge Distillation with Affordable Cost</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Knowledge distillation (KD) is one of the most powerful methods to alleviate the accuracy degradation after model compression.
However, there are several limitations of KD, especially for hidden-states KD on large-scale language models:
(1) KD needs to hold a teacher and a student model together during the training, which dramatically increases the memory and compute cost;
(2) KD usually requires full training of the student model.
Therefore, several copies (gradient, first/second order momentum) of the weight parameters need to be stored in memory to update the model;
(3) KD generally requires original training data, which sometimes are not accessible due to privacy/confidential issues.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To address those limitations, we present our layer-by-layer distillation (LKD) algorithm.
Assume the target model for quantization has <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> transformer blocks, <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>, …, <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{N}</annotation></semantics></math>, the accessible dataset has input <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="({\bm{X}},~{\bm{Y}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑿</mi><mo rspace="0.497em">,</mo><mi>𝒀</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">({\bm{X}},~{\bm{Y}})</annotation></semantics></math>, which can be the original training data or datasets from other resources.
Our LKD quantizes the network layer-by-layer and uses its original (i.e., unquantized) version as the teacher model.
More specifically, assume layer <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> is going to be quantized, and its quantized version is <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{L}_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>L</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{L}_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Then we use the output of the <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{k-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{k-1}</annotation></semantics></math> (i.e., by running inference on <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> over the first <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k-1</annotation></semantics></math> layers)
as the input of <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{L}_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>L</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{L}_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>, measure the difference, and do the model update to <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e.,</p>
<table id="S4.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\small\mathcal{L}_{LKD,k}=MSE\left(L_{k}\cdot L_{k-1}\cdot L_{k-2}\cdot...\cdot L_{1}({\bm{X}})-\widehat{L}_{k}\cdot L_{k-1}\cdot L_{k-2}\cdot...\cdot L_{1}({\bm{X}})\right)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">L</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">𝑿</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">−</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.900em">L</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathsize="0.900em">k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" mathsize="0.900em" mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">L</mi><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">k</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">−</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em" mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">L</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">𝑿</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo></mrow><annotation L_{1}({\bm{X}})\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="MSE" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>E</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">MSE</annotation></semantics></math> is the mean square loss, and it can be also replaced by other losses (e.g., KL divergence) as well.
As can be seen,
(1) our LKD does not need to hold a separate teacher as we use the same <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{k-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{k-1}</annotation></semantics></math> for both teacher/student model. As such, the only extra model cost we have is <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>;
(2) the memory overhead of optimizer states are significantly reduced as the only optimizing layer is <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>;
(3) as we never optimize the end-to-end model, the training does not depend on the label anymore.
Later, we will show that LKD does not rely on the original training data in Section <a href="#S5.SS6" title="5.6 No Access to The Original Training Data ‣ 5 Results ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Quantization-Optimized Transformer Kernels</h3>

<figure id="S4.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2206.01861v1/operator_fusion.svg" id="S4.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:471/57;" width="471" height="57"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>
The illustration of normal (left) and our fused (right) INT8 GeMM.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Both optimizing the inference latency and model size is crucial for serving large-scale transformer models in practice.
During inference, the batch size is often relatively small, so the inference latency of the model primarily depends on the time of loading inference needed data from the main memory.
By quantizing the weights and activations to lower precision, we reduce the data volume needed to load those data, which allows more effective use of memory bandwidth and higher loading throughput.
However, simply converting weights/activations to INT8 does not guarantee improved latency because there are additional data movement overhead associated with quantization/dequantization operations as shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 4.3 Quantization-Optimized Transformer Kernels ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> (red box).
Such an overhead becomes expensive and in some cases surpasses the performance benefits of using low precision.
To reap the accuracy improvement from token-wise quantization while obtaining improved latency, we now present our optimizations that maximize the memory bandwidth utilization to speed up inference latency for ZeroQuant.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">CUTLASS INT8 GeMM</span> To support INT8 computation, we use CUTLASS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite> INT8 GeMM implementation tuned for different batch sizes.
Unlike standard GPU backend library, such as cuDNN, using CUTLASS allows us to more flexibly fuse quantization operation before and after GeMM to reduce kernel launching and data-movement overhead.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Fusing Token-wise Activation Quantization</span> Token-wise quantization/dequantization introduce many additional operations that lead to extra data movement cost.
To eliminate these cost, we use <em id="S4.SS3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">kernel fusion</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">67</a>]</cite> to fuse quantization operation for activation with its previous element-wise and/or reduction operations such as bias-add, GeLU, and LayerNorm into a single operator, as illustrated by the green box in Figure <a href="#S4.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 4.3 Quantization-Optimized Transformer Kernels ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.
For the dequantization operation (e.g., dequantizing the integer output from the GeMM operator), we similarly fuse it with our custom GeMM schedule to avoid additional read/write accesses to the main memory as illustrated by the blue box in Figure <a href="#S4.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 4.3 Quantization-Optimized Transformer Kernels ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">By doing the above optimizations,
we are able to show significant latency reduction for BERT and GPT-3-style models in Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Results ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.
Please see Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Details about System Optimization ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a> for more details about our system optimization.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>
Result of BERT<math id="S4.T2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{{base}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{{base}}}</annotation></semantics></math> on the development set of GLUE benchmark (except WNLI).
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>]</cite><sup id="S4.T2.4" class="ltx_sup">+</sup> uses 128 groups for weight matrix which is hard to get GPU acceleration.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite><sup id="S4.T2.5" class="ltx_sup">∗</sup> uses mixed INT8 and FP16 activation, and it directly reports the average metric of MNLI/MRPC/QQP/STS-B, which is basically the average of the two metrics we used for our runs.
</figcaption>

<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Results</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experimental Details</span>
To evaluate the proposed ZeroQuant, we test it on both BERT and GPT-3 models.
For BERT, we tested both BERT<math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{{base}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{{base}}}</annotation></semantics></math> and BERT<math id="S5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{large}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>large</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{large}}</annotation></semantics></math> on GLUE benchmark;
and for GPT-3-style models, we tested the GPT-3<math id="S5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{350M}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>350M</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{350M}}</annotation></semantics></math> (i.e., GPT-3-style model with 350M parameters) and GPT-3<math id="S5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{1.3B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>1.3B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{1.3B}}</annotation></semantics></math> (i.e., GPT-3-style model with 1.3B parameters) on 20 zero-shot evaluation tasks, including 19 accuracy-based tasks and 1 language modeling generation task.
To illustrate the scalability of the proposed ZeroQuant, we also directly apply it to two of the largest open-sourced GPT-3-style models, i.e., GPT-J<math id="S5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{6B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>6B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{6B}}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">66</a>]</cite> and GPT-NeoX<math id="S5.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{20B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>20B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{20B}}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>.
We use a fixed set of hyperparameters for all the LKD-related experiments even though tuning them may benefit our results.
Please see Appendix <a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 Details of Main Result ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a> for more training details and see Appendix <a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 Accuracy reported for BERT on GLUE ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a> for the reported metrics for BERT.
To provide a comprehensive study, we also include a tuning result in Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Tuned Results on BERT ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a> on BERT and an ablation study for different proposed components in Section <a href="#S5.SS5" title="5.5 Ablation Study of Different Components ‣ 5 Results ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Notation Explanation</span>
We use WxAy to represent using x-bit for weight quantization and y-bit for activation quantization.
Unless specific explanation, for W4/8, we quantize the MHSA’s weight to INT8 and FFC’s weight to INT4;
for A8/16, we use FP16 activation for self-attention calculation (i.e., the GeMM related to <math id="S5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bm{W}}_{q/k/v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝑾</mi><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{W}}_{q/k/v}</annotation></semantics></math>) and use INT8 for the rest calculation.
We use ZeroQuant to represent the method with only fine-grained quantization schemes and use ZeroQuant-LKD to represent the method with both fine-grained quantization schemes and LKD.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Main Results of BERT</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">BERT<math id="S5.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{{base}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{{base}}}</annotation></semantics></math></span>
We report the results of BERT<math id="S5.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{{base}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{{base}}}</annotation></semantics></math> in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Quantization-Optimized Transformer Kernels ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.
For W8A8, the average accuracy of PTQ degrades more than 10 points.
However, ZeroQuant can achieve 83.75 scores, which is only 0.2 lower than baseline.
Particularly, as ZeroQuant has no activation range calibration phase, the cost of ZeroQuant is <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> which is even cheaper than standard PTQ.
As compared to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>, our method achieves a better average score (1.29 higher).
Meanwhile, as compared to INT8 activation used in ZeroQuant, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite> uses mixed INT8 and FP16 activation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We also compare our method with our internal trained QAT and other QAT works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>, <a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">76</a>]</cite>.
As can be seen, with comparable accuracy results as those QAT methods, ZeroQuant can save the retraining cost from 2900s to 0s for INT8 quantization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For the more aggressive weight quantization with minimal (or no) training quantization, i.e., W4/8A16, PTQ fully loses all accuracy (pure random prediction).
However, ZeroQuant can still achieve an 81.65 average score.
On top of ZeroQuant, if we add our LKD, the accuracy can be further boosted to 82.35 with a cost of 31s per task using only a single GPU, which is 93.5x cheaper than INT8 QAT quantization.
We also test ZeroQuant and ZeroQuant-LKD under the W4/8A8 quantization scheme and both of them achieve similar accuracy performance as W4/8A16.
If hyper-parameter tuning is applied to LKD, ZeroQuant-LKD can achieve an 83.22 average score under W4/8A8, which is similar to QAT’s W8A8 result.
Please see Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Tuned Results on BERT ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a> for more details.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">BERT<math id="S5.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{large}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">large</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{large}}</annotation></semantics></math></span>
We test our methods on BERT<math id="S5.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{large}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>large</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{large}}</annotation></semantics></math> as well and the results are shown in Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.1 Main Results of BERT ‣ 5 Results ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.
Similar to BERT<math id="S5.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{{base}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{{base}}}</annotation></semantics></math>, ZeroQuant achieves much better accuracy than PTQ methods.
As compared to QAT methods, ZeroQuant has comparable results on larger datasets (like MNLI/QQP) and has better performance on small tasks (e.e., CoLA/MRPC/RTE).
We actually tune QAT for multiple learning rates but cannot get even better performance for those small tasks (see Appendix <a href="#A6" title='Appendix F QAT on BERT_"large" ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers' class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a> for more details).</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">For more aggressive quantization schemes, like W4/8A16 and W4/8A8, ZeroQuant and ZeroQuant-LKD still achieve good accuracy except for RTE but the model size is about 3x smaller than FP16 counterpart.
This is aligned with the INT8 QAT results, which lose significantly more accuracy on RTE.
Thanks to the lightweight cost of LKD, it only takes about 550s to finish each task even on BERT<math id="S5.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{large}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>large</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{large}}</annotation></semantics></math>, which is 13x cheaper than QAT.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>
Result of BERT<math id="S5.T3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{large}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>large</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{large}}</annotation></semantics></math> on the development set of GLUE benchmark (except WNLI).
<sup id="S5.T3.3" class="ltx_sup">+</sup>We extensively tuned the learning rate for QAT (see Appendix <a href="#A6" title='Appendix F QAT on BERT_"large" ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers' class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a> for more details).

<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Main Results of GPT-3-style Models</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPT-3<math id="S5.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{350M}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">350M</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{350M}}</annotation></semantics></math></span>
We first test ZeroQuant and ZeroQuant-LKD on GPT-3<math id="S5.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{350M}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>350M</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{350M}}</annotation></semantics></math> and report the result in Table <a href="#S5.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 5.1 Main Results of BERT ‣ 5 Results ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.
The first interesting finding of zero-shot evaluation on GPT-3-stype models is that the accuracy performance of accuracy-based tasks is more tolerant to quantization than generation tasks.
For instance, W8A8 PTQ has a 1.1% average accuracy drop on 19 accuracy-based tasks as compared to 4.7 points loss on Wikitext-2.
Comparing ZeroQuant with PTQ using W8A8, we can reduce the accuracy gap from 1.1% to 0.2% and the perplexity (PPL) gap from 4.7 to 0.2 with no activation range calibration cost.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For W4/8A16 quantization scheme, PTQ can hardly predict reasonable answers for the majority of tasks and its generation performance on Wikitext-2 is fully crashed.
As a comparison, ZeroQuant still achieves non-trivial performance on some tasks but its generation performance significantly degrades on Wikitext-2.
LKD brings a significant performance boost for this W4/8A16 setting.
Note that ZeroQuant-LKD increases the accuracy from 33.5 to 37.0 and decreases the PPL from 88.6 to 30.6 compared to ZeroQuant,
and the entire cost of this is just 3.1 hours on a single A100 GPU.
Note that this is about 0.027% GPU hours of the full pretraining cost (128 A100 GPUs for 32 hours).
Similar to W4/8A16, ZeroQuant-LKD achieves much better performance than ZeroQuant on W4/8A8 by using the lightweight LKD.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T5" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span>
Post training quantization result of GPT-3<math id="S5.T5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{1.3B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>1.3B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{1.3B}}</annotation></semantics></math> on 20 zero-shot evaluation datasets.
Please see Table <a href="#A8.T2" title="Table H.2 ‣ Appendix H Full Zero-shot Evaluation of GPT-3-style Models ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.2</span></a> for the results of all 20 tasks.
</figcaption>
<div id="S5.T5.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:689.2pt;height:110.4pt;vertical-align:-52.7pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(0.0pt,0.0pt) scale(1,1) ;">
<p id="S5.T5.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.T5.2.1.1" class="ltx_text">
<span id="S5.T5.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<span id="S5.T5.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S5.T5.2.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt">Precision (Method)</span>
<span id="S5.T5.2.1.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt">Lambada (<math id="S5.T5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\uparrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↑</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\uparrow</annotation></semantics></math>)</span>
<span id="S5.T5.2.1.1.1.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt">PIQA (<math id="S5.T5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\uparrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↑</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\uparrow</annotation></semantics></math>)</span>

<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPT-3<math id="S5.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{1.3B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">1.3B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{1.3B}}</annotation></semantics></math></span>
The results of GPT-3<math id="S5.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{1.3B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>1.3B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{1.3B}}</annotation></semantics></math> are shown in Table <a href="#S5.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 5.2 Main Results of GPT-3-style Models ‣ 5 Results ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.
Similar to GPT-3<math id="S5.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{350M}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>350M</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{350M}}</annotation></semantics></math>, for W8A8, ZeroQuant has much better performance than PTQ with less no activation calibration cost, particularly for the generation task Wikitext-2 (3.2 points lower).
Also, for W4/8 quantization, LKD can bring non-trivial performance gain for ZeroQuant.
The cost of LKD is about 0.02% of the full pre-training cost (128 A100 GPUs for 120 hours)</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Latency Reduction of BERT and GPT-3-style Models</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare the inference speed of BERT between FP16 and our INT8 versions in Table <a href="#S5.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 5.2 Main Results of GPT-3-style Models ‣ 5 Results ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> on a single 40G-A100 GPU.
Using our efficient quantization kernel implementation and operator fusion, the INT8 model can achieve 2.27–5.19x speedup on BERT<math id="S5.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{{base}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{{base}}}</annotation></semantics></math> and 2.47–5.01x on BERT<math id="S5.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{large}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>large</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{large}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We also include the latency comparison of GPT-3-style models between FP16 and our INT8 version.
Particularly, we use the model to generate the first 50 tokens based on a given text and measure the average latency.
Our INT8 model leads to 4.16x/4.06x speedup for GPT-3<math id="S5.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{350M}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>350M</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{350M}}</annotation></semantics></math>/GPT-3<math id="S5.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{1.3B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>1.3B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{1.3B}}</annotation></semantics></math> as compared to the FP16 counterpart.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>A Showcase of GPT-J<math id="S5.SS4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{6B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>6B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{6B}}</annotation></semantics></math> and GPT-NeoX<math id="S5.SS4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{20B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>20B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{20B}}</annotation></semantics></math></h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To demonstrate the scalability of ZeroQuant, we applied it to two of the largest open-sourced models, i.e., GPT-J<math id="S5.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{6B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>6B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{6B}}</annotation></semantics></math> and GPT-NeoX<math id="S5.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{20B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>20B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{20B}}</annotation></semantics></math>, which have 6B and 20B parameters separately.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We report the results of GPT-J<math id="S5.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{6B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>6B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{6B}}</annotation></semantics></math> in Table <a href="#S5.T8" title='Table 8 ‣ 5.4 A Showcase of GPT-J_"6B" and GPT-NeoX_"20B" ‣ 5 Results ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers' class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> on three generation datasets, i.e., PTB <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite>, Wikitext-2, and Wikitext-103 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite>.
As can be seen, as compared to FP16 precision, ZeroQuant achieves similar PPL on all three different tasks.
To compare the latency, we again use the average latency number to generate the first 50 tokens.
Our W8A8 can get up to 3.67x speedup compared to the FP16 version.</p>
</div>

<span id="S5.T8.p4.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
