<span id="S5.T8.p4.1.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:1.5pt;padding-right:1.5pt;">Precision</span>
<span id="S5.T8.p4.1.1.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:1.5pt;padding-right:1.5pt;">Lambada</span>
<span id="S5.T8.p4.1.1.1.1.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:1.5pt;padding-right:1.5pt;">PIQA</span>
<span id="S5.T8.p4.1.1.1.1.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:1.5pt;padding-right:1.5pt;">Ave. 19 Tasks</span>
<span id="S5.T8.p4.1.1.1.1.1.5" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:1.5pt;padding-right:1.5pt;">Latency</span></span>
<span id="S5.T8.p4.1.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S5.T8.p4.1.1.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:1.5pt;padding-right:1.5pt;">W16A16</span>
<span id="S5.T8.p4.1.1.1.1.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:1.5pt;padding-right:1.5pt;">71.7</span>
<span id="S5.T8.p4.1.1.1.1.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:1.5pt;padding-right:1.5pt;">77.7</span>
<span id="S5.T8.p4.1.1.1.1.2.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:1.5pt;padding-right:1.5pt;">50.5</span>
<span id="S5.T8.p4.1.1.1.1.2.5" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:1.5pt;padding-right:1.5pt;">2<math id="S5.T8.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>65ms (1x)</span></span>
<span id="S5.T8.p4.1.1.1.1.3" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S5.T8.p4.1.1.1.1.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:1.5pt;padding-right:1.5pt;">W8A8/16</span>
<span id="S5.T8.p4.1.1.1.1.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:1.5pt;padding-right:1.5pt;">71.9</span>
<span id="S5.T8.p4.1.1.1.1.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:1.5pt;padding-right:1.5pt;">78.3</span>
<span id="S5.T8.p4.1.1.1.1.3.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:1.5pt;padding-right:1.5pt;">50.4</span>
<span id="S5.T8.p4.1.1.1.1.3.5" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:1.5pt;padding-right:1.5pt;">1<math id="S5.T8.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>25ms (5.2x)</span></span>
</span></span></p>
</span></div>
</div>
</div></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To quantize GPT-NeoX<math id="S5.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{20B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>20B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{20B}}</annotation></semantics></math> to W8A8 for all GeMMs, the accuracy significantly decreases.
We retrieve the quantization of each weight matrix and of each activation, and finally find out that the activation quantization for the attention calculation (i.e., the input of self-attention) causes the accuracy loss.
We conjecture that this is because of the sensitivity of the self-attention module for extra-large models (20B) but cannot verify this for other models due to the lack of open-sourced extra-large models and the full evaluation pipeline.
As such, we leave the input activation for self-attention in FP16 and quantize the rest to INT8.
The results are shown in Table <a href="#S5.T8" title='Table 8 ‣ 5.4 A Showcase of GPT-J_"6B" and GPT-NeoX_"20B" ‣ 5 Results ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers' class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>.
Our W8A8/16 achieves similar accuracy performance but can reduce both the GPU resource requirement (from 2 A100 GPUs to 1) and the latency from 65ms to 25ms,
which together lead to 5.2x better throughput/efficiency.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.5 </span>Ablation Study of Different Components</h3>

<div id="S5.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To investigate the performance gain of each component we introduced in Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Methodology ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, i.e., group-wise weight quantization, token-wise activation quantization, and lightweight layer-by-layer knowledge distillation, we here do an ablation study on BERT<math id="S5.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{large}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>large</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{large}}</annotation></semantics></math> with W4/8A8.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We present the results in Table <a href="#S5.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ 5.5 Ablation Study of Different Components ‣ 5 Results ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>.
As can be seen, group-wise weight quantization boosts the accuracy (random-guess prediction) from PTQ to a non-trivial result (66.52).
Further adding token-wise quantization improves 14.54 points accuracy performance.
On top of those (i.e., ZeroQuant), LKD further brings a 0.56 point gain.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T9" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 9: </span>

The quantization scheme used here is W4/8A8.
Here, GP is the abbreviation of group-wise weight quantization, TQ is the abbreviation of token-wise activation quantization.

<span id="S5.T10.2.1.1.1.3.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">59.3</span>
<span id="S5.T10.2.1.1.1.3.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">29.2</span>
<span id="S5.T10.2.1.1.1.3.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">50.5</span>
<span id="S5.T10.2.1.1.1.3.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">64.9</span>
<span id="S5.T10.2.1.1.1.3.8" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">34.5</span>
<span id="S5.T10.2.1.1.1.3.9" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">40.6</span></span>
<span id="S5.T10.2.1.1.1.4" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S5.T10.2.1.1.1.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">ZeroQuant-LKD</span>
<span id="S5.T10.2.1.1.1.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">Wikipedia</span>
<span id="S5.T10.2.1.1.1.4.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">33.9</span>
<span id="S5.T10.2.1.1.1.4.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">62.4</span>
<span id="S5.T10.2.1.1.1.4.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">28.0</span>
<span id="S5.T10.2.1.1.1.4.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">52.7</span>
<span id="S5.T10.2.1.1.1.4.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">69.5</span>
<span id="S5.T10.2.1.1.1.4.8" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">36.2</span>
<span id="S5.T10.2.1.1.1.4.9" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">30.4</span></span>
<span id="S5.T10.2.1.1.1.5" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S5.T10.2.1.1.1.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb">ZeroQuant-LKD</span>

<span id="S5.T10.2.1.1.1.5.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">28.2</span>

<span id="S5.T10.2.1.1.1.5.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">68.5</span>
<span id="S5.T10.2.1.1.1.5.8" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">36.6</span>
<span id="S5.T10.2.1.1.1.5.9" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">31.1</span></span>
</span></span></p>
</span></div>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.6 </span>No Access to The Original Training Data</h3>

<div id="S5.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As mentioned in previous sections, the original training data are oftentimes hard to access due to the privacy and/or confidential issues.
Therefore, we here study the performance of our LKD when there is no direct access to the original training data.
As the distillation objective of our LKD does not depend on the label, the training data used for LKD can be very flexible.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We compare the performance of GPT-3<math id="S5.SS6.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{350M}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>350M</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{350M}}</annotation></semantics></math> on W4/8A8 quantization scheme using three different training data resources, i.e., random data (using random integer number to generate token ids), Wikipedia (using Huggingface to get the data<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
            <a href="https://huggingface.co/datasets/wikipedia" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://huggingface.co/datasets/wikipedia</a></span></span></span>), and original PILE dataset.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The results are shown in Table <a href="#S5.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ 5.5 Ablation Study of Different Components ‣ 5 Results ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>.
Compared to ZeroQuant, LKD using random data can boost the accuracy by 1.1% and reduce the PPL from 92.1 to 40.6.
The reason why random data can still significantly improve the performance is that LKD does not optimize the end-to-end pipeline and it only layer-by-layer learns the internal dependency from the teacher model.
Therefore, random data can also provide meaningful information.
Using Wikipedia data from Huggingface can further improve the accuracy to 36.2 and reduce the PPL to 30.4, which is comparable to the results using the original data.
This indicates that a clean text dataset can be used for LKD when we do not have access to the original full dataset.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusions</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">With the rapid growth of large model sizes, we have reach a point to consider how to serve those models in practice.
Although several works demonstrate that post-training quantization can be applied to BERT models, to the best of our knowledge, there have been no existing works on (1) billion-scale GPT-3-style models, (2) ultra-low precision post-training quantization, and (3) end-to-end solution of how to efficiently serve the quantized model online.
In this work, we offer fine-grained compression schemes for both weight and activations to enable INT8 quantization for up to 20B-scale models (GPT-NeoX<math id="S6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{20B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>20B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{20B}}</annotation></semantics></math>).
We also offer a novel affordable layer-by-layer knowledge distillation for ultra-low precision quantization, which leads to 3x model size reduction compared to FP16 model while achieving minimal accuracy degradation.
Furthermore, we provide a system backend support and show up to 5.19x speedup on BERT models and 5.2x better efficiency on GPT-NeoX<math id="S6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{20B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>20B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{20B}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Background</h2>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Transformer Architecture</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The transformer architecture usually has three components: an embedding layer, a stack of encoder/decoder layers, and a final classifier.
In this paper, we focus on quantizing the encoder/decoder layers, i.e., the transformer block, because it is often the most memory and compute intensive components in the entire architecture. With a transformer block, there are two sub-layers, the multi-head self-attention (MHSA) and the feed-forward connection (FFC).
We give a short review later and please refer to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">64</a>]</cite> for more details. At high level, transformer models can be broadly categorized to three branches: encoder-only models (BERT) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>]</cite>, decoder-only models (GPT-3-style) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>]</cite>, and encoder-decoder models (T5) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>.
In this paper, we focus on encoder-only and decoder-only models but our approach can be applied to encoder-decoder models as well.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2206.01861v1/transformer_block.svg" id="A1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:471/104;" width="471" height="104"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure A.1: </span>
The illustration of a Transformer-block.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Transformer Block</h4>

<div id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Assume the input of an encoder layer is <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bm{X}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝑿</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{X}}</annotation></semantics></math>,
the query, key, value, attention output, FFC dense, and FFC output matrices are <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bm{W}}_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝑾</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{W}}_{q}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bm{W}}_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝑾</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{W}}_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bm{W}}_{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝑾</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{W}}_{v}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bm{W}}_{o}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝑾</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{W}}_{o}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bm{W}}_{h-4h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝑾</mi><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{W}}_{h-4h}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bm{W}}_{4h-h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝑾</mi><mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{W}}_{4h-h}</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively.
Then the forward propagation of a transformer-block is illustrated in Figure <a href="#A1.F1" title="Figure A.1 ‣ A.1 Transformer Architecture ‣ Appendix A Background ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a>, where LN is the layer normalization, Softmax is the softmax operator, and GeLU is the activation function.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Quantization Background</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Quantization maps high-precision numbers, e.g., FP16/FP32, to its low-precision counterpart, e.g., INT4/INT8, to reduce the model footprint and improve the compute performance.
In this work, we use uniform symmetric scalar quantizers.
That is to say, if we have a vector/matrix, <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{x}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{x}}</annotation></semantics></math>, the quantization is applied as</p>
<table id="A1.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{x}}_{quantize}=round\left(clamp(\frac{{\mathbf{x}}}{S},-2^{bit-1},2^{bit-1}-1)\right)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>z</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mfrac><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>S</mi></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{x}}_{quantize}=round\left(clamp(\frac{{\mathbf{x}}}{S},-2^{bit-1},2^{bit-1}-1)\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bit" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bit</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of bit we use to represent the quantized value, and <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> is the scaling factor.
For weight matrix quantization, <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> is generally computed as
<math id="A1.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S=max\left(abs({\mathbf{x}})\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S=max\left(abs({\mathbf{x}})\right)</annotation></semantics></math>,
since the weight matrix is static during inference.
On the other hand, activations’ range is dynamic during inference so that an accurate <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> requires dynamic calculation during inference.
However, to achieve best latency reduction, coarse-grained static quantization is usually applied in practice, where <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> is calibrated using training data (e.g., momentum based averaging) and fixed during inference <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>.
Although static quantization achieves better latency reduction, it also limits the quantization representation for activations, which is discussed in Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Background and Challenge ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Experimental Details</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Details of PTQ on BERT and GPT</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For BERT, we use a batch size of 32 and sequence length 128 to calibrate the range of activations.
In order to capture the dynamic range, we use 0.95 momentum with 100 iterations, i.e.,</p>
<table id="A2.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A2.Ex1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A2.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle x_{max}=0.95x_{max}+0.05max(x_{current-iteration})," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>0.95</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>0.05</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle x_{max}=0.95x_{max}+0.05max(x_{current-iteration}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="A2.Ex2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A2.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle x_{min}=0.95x_{min}+0.05min(x_{current-iteration})." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>0.95</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>0.05</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle x_{min}=0.95x_{min}+0.05min(x_{current-iteration}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">For GPT-3-style models, we use the same momentum method but change the batch size to 8 with sequence length 2048.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Details of Main Result</h3>

<section id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">BERT</h4>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">BERT models are trained using the code-base from Huggingface <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">72</a>]</cite>.
We show our ZeroQuant method on BERT<math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{{base}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{{base}}}</annotation></semantics></math> and BERT<math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{large}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>large</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{large}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We use the same lower-case tokenizer in BERT<math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{large}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>large</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{large}}</annotation></semantics></math> instead of the cased tokenizer in the original paper <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>.
When fine-tuning on GLUE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">65</a>]</cite> tasks ((i.e.,
MRPC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>,
STS-B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>,
SST-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">58</a>]</cite>, QNLI <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite>, QQP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>, MNLI <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">70</a>]</cite>, CoLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">69</a>]</cite>, RTE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>).<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
                
                
                
              We exclude WNLI <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite> since its results are not stable <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>.</span></span></span>), we follow the instruction from Huggingface Transformer Library <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">72</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For ZeroQuant and ZeroQuant-LKD, we use 48 groups for group-wise weight quantization on BERT<math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{{base}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{{base}}}</annotation></semantics></math> and 64 groups for group-wise weight quantization on BERT<math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{large}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>large</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{large}}</annotation></semantics></math>, for all the weight matrices.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For LKD, we use 100 iterations with batch size 32 and sequence length 128 for BERT<math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{{base}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{{base}}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and we use 400 iterations for BERT<math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{large}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>large</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{large}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We fix the learning rate as 5e-6 for both models on all tasks.
However, tuning them may favor ZeroQuant.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">All the models are trained using a single 40G-A100 GPU (Azure ND A100 instances).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">GPT-3-style Models</h4>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All GPT-3-style models used in the paper are trained using DeepSpeed <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>]</cite> and Megatron-DeepSpeed Library <span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
                
                
                
              <a href="https://github.com/microsoft/Megatron-DeepSpeed" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/microsoft/Megatron-DeepSpeed</a></span></span></span>.
The pretraining data are from PILE dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>, and the training pipeline and hyperparameters are based on the Megatron-DeepSpeed repository.
We use 128 A100 GPUs (Azure ND A100 instances) to do the pretraining.
It takes about 32 hours to finish the training of GPT-3<math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{350M}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>350M</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{350M}}</annotation></semantics></math> and 120 hours of GPT-3<math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{1.3B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>1.3B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{1.3B}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We evaluate our results on 20 zero-shot evaluation tasks, including 19 accuracy evaluation tasks (i.e., HellaSwag <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">77</a>]</cite>, LAMBADA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>]</cite>, TriviaQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>, WebQS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>, Winogrande <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>]</cite>, PIQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">62</a>]</cite>, ARC (Challenge/Easy) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>, ANLI (R1/R2/R3) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">71</a>]</cite>, OpenBookQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite>, RACE-h <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite>, BoolQ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>, Copa <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>, RTE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>, WSC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>, MultiRC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">73</a>]</cite>, ReCoRD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">78</a>]</cite>) and 1 language modeling generation task (i.e., Wikitext-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite>).</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For ZeroQuant and ZeroQuant-LKD, we use 64/128 groups for group-wise weight quantization on GPT-3<math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{350M}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>350M</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{350M}}</annotation></semantics></math>/GPT-3<math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{1.3B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>1.3B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{1.3B}}</annotation></semantics></math> for all the weight matrices.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For LKD, we use 1600 iterations with batch size 8 and sequence length 2048 for both GPT-3<math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{350M}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>350M</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{350M}}</annotation></semantics></math> and GPT-3<math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{1.3B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>1.3B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{1.3B}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We fix the learning rate as 5e-6 for both models.
However, tuning them may favor ZeroQuant.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">All the quantized models are trained using a single 40G-A100 GPU (Azure ND A100 instances).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span>Accuracy reported for BERT on GLUE</h3>

<div id="A2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report the performance metric for BERT on GLUE based on Table <a href="#A2.T1" title="Table B.1 ‣ B.3 Accuracy reported for BERT on GLUE ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>.
For the average score, if the task only has one metric, we use it for the final result; if the task has two metrics, we compute the average of the two metrics first and use it for the final average score.
For instance, the score of MRPC used to compute the final average is the mean of its accuracy and F1 score.</p>
</div>

<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>PTQ challenge of BERT<math id="A3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{{base}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{{base}}}</annotation></semantics></math></h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">From Table <a href="#A3.T1" title='Table C.1 ‣ Appendix C PTQ challenge of BERT_"base" ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers' class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1</span></a>, we observe similar results as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>, where the accuracy degradation of INT8 quantization is mainly from activation quantization.
Specifically, there is a negligible accuracy drop from INT8 weight quantization (i.e., the row of W8A16).
However, with sole INT8 activation (i.e., the row of W16A8), the accuracy decreases from 84.06 to 79.61.
Besides, we also push the weight quantization to a mixed-precision setting with INT4 for weights in FFC and INT8 for weights in MHSA (i.e., the row of W4/8A16).
This ultra-low precision quantization leads the model to be purely random without meaning prediction.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table C.1: </span>
Post training quantization results of BERT<math id="A3.T1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{{base}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{{base}}}</annotation></semantics></math> on development sets of the GLUE benchmark (except WNLI).
Here WxAy means x-bit for weight quantization and y-bit for activation quantization.
Particularly, for W4/8, we quantize the MHSA’s weight to INT8 and FFC’s weight to INT4.
Please see Appendix <a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 Accuracy reported for BERT on GLUE ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a> for the reported metrics.
</figcaption>

</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Details about System Optimization</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">By having the weight and activation quantization, we can use the GeMM schedule that exploits the INT8 Tensor-core units which
provide 2x/4x more compute efficiency compared to the FP16/FP32 Tensor cores.
For this purpose, we adapt the CUTLASS library to produce multiple schedules based on the input sizes we are considering in our application, such as the batch size, sequence length, and the Transformer hidden dimension.
To achieve the best latency, we also develop our own efficient parallel implementation of the quantization operator on GPU.
During the inference run-time, based on the total batch size (<math id="A4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="batch\times seq_{l}en" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">batch\times seq_{l}en</annotation></semantics></math>), we choose the schedule that results in the lowest possible padding when performing the Tensor-core matrix-multiplication operations.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To find the best schedule for the GeMM operation, we use the CUTLASS profiler tool that explores the tiling dimensions on
the thread-blocks, WARPs, and WMMA (Tensor cores), as the three compute hierarchies available within the Ampere GPU architecture.
Then, we find the best schedule by sorting the tile-based schedule based on either peak throughput achieved on the large-batch case, or
the maximum memory bandwidth taken from the main memory when the batch size is small.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">However, there are still several challenges we need to address which are discussed below.</p>
</div>
<section id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Operation Fusion for Token-wise Activation Quantization.</h4>

<div id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">One of the main challenges of our quantization scheme is how to efficiently quantize hidden states before the GeMM operation.
In order to remove the overhead, we fuse the activation quantization with its associated element-wise and/or reduction-based operations such as bias-addition, GELY, and LayerNorm.
This is due to the fact that
each SM takes care of one row (token) of the activation and therefore, we can reuse the computation from the thread registers
and compute the quantization scale, avoiding the data movement between GPU kernels and main memory.
Moreover, by converting data from FP16 to INT8, we can utilize the memory bandwidth twice, further improving the inference latency and throughput.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Dequantization Associated with GeMM Schedule</h4>

<div id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To utilize the output of integer output from GeMM operator in the following operators, one important step is to dequantize the output by using the scaling factor of the weight and activations.
This dequantization step generally introduces extra overhead for quantized network inference due to the data movement.
As such, we add a custom epilogue, which converts the final accumulated result (from INT32 format) of each row and column of the output to the
real value (in FP16 format), using corresponding floating-point quantization scales computed from weight and activation group-wise quantization.
By fusing the dequantization with GeMM schedule, we ensure that there is no overhead exposed by using the INT8 operations while producing the
FP16 results that are used in the following operation.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Furthermore, to effectively combine dequantization with the GeMM operation,
we read the two groups of quantization scales for the activation and weight matrices in advance prior to completion of the multiplication of the output matrix.
Doing so, we overlap the reading of the extra quantization parameters with the
GeMM computation and the GeMM-plus-dequantization can seamlessly work together without stalling the inference pipeline.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Cuda Graph Enhanced Small Model Inference.</h4>

<div id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As the execution time for specific kernels reduce by optimizing the throughput using the INT8 inference pipeline, the overhead of launching
the GPU kernels and the CPU-to-GPU communication become a major bottleneck mostly on small-scale models.
To address this issue, we add the CUDA-Graph support to our inference pipeline that reduces the CPU overhead, by storing the trace of the kernels launched during the inference
forward computation, and creating the computation-graph to be reused in the next call to the inference pipeline.
Thus, after storing the graph for
the first time, we can replay the graph for the following requests, which substantially improves the performance especially on small models, such
as BERT<math id="A4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{{base}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{{base}}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
For a fair comparison, we also enable Cuda Graph for FP16 baseline.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Tuned Results on BERT</h2>

<div id="A5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As mentioned in the main text and Appendix <a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 Details of Main Result ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a>, we use the same set of hyperparameters for BERT.
However, tuning them can significantly boost the performance for ZeroQuant.
Here, we tune two hyperparameters, i.e., the learning rate and the number of iterations in order to show the best possible performance of ZeroQuant on both BERT<math id="A5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{{base}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{{base}}}</annotation></semantics></math> and BERT<math id="A5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{large}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>large</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{large}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Particularly, we choose learning rate from the set {1e-6, 2e-6, 5e-6, 1e-5}, and choose number of iterations from the set {0, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800, 1600}.
Thanks to the lightweight of LKD, the total tuning time for BERT<math id="A5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{{base}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{{base}}}</annotation></semantics></math> (including all data loading time, evaluation time, tokenization time, all three quantization schemes, etc) is around 4.5 hours on 8 40G-A100 GPUs (i.e., 36 GPU hours), and the tuning time for BERT<math id="A5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{large}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>large</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{large}}</annotation></semantics></math> is around 16 hours on 8 40G-A100 GPUs (i.e., 128 GPU hours).</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We summarize the best results in the Table <a href="#A5.T1" title="Table E.1 ‣ Appendix E Tuned Results on BERT ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1</span></a> and <a href="#A5.T2" title="Table E.2 ‣ Appendix E Tuned Results on BERT ‣ ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>

Result of BERT<math id="A5.T2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{large}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>large</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{large}}</annotation></semantics></math> on the development set of GLUE benchmark (except WNLI).
Here WxAy means x-bit for weight quantization and y-bit for activation quantization.
Particularly, for W4/8, we quantize the MHSA’s weight to INT8 and FFC’s weight to INT4.

<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>QAT on BERT<math id="A6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{large}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>large</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{large}}</annotation></semantics></math></h2>

<div id="A6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use four different learning rates for QAT on BERT<math id="A6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{large}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>large</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{large}}</annotation></semantics></math>, {5e-6, 1e-5, 2e-5, 5e-5}.
The final results we reported in the paper are chosen from the best single run among those four different learning rates.
However, even with such tuning, we are not able to get good performance for BERT<math id="A6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{large}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>large</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{large}}</annotation></semantics></math> on RTE.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Also, note that the time cost we used in the main text is based on a single run.
if we consider the tuning cost, the total time will be <math id="A6.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4\times 7181" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>7181</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4\times 7181</annotation></semantics></math>s</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A7" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix G </span>Limitations and Future Work</h2>

<div id="A7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We believe it is critical for every work to clearly state its limitations, especially in this area.
One limitation is that in this work we only focused on natural language models, but it would
be interesting to see how ZeroQuant would perform for computer vision models.
We leave this as a future work.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Another limitation is that we can only verify the scalability of ZeroQuant up to 20B scale models.
If there are new releases of larger open-sourced models, it would be great to test ZeroQuant on those larger models as well.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Third, in this paper, we found out that the activation input of self-attention is more sensitive for quantization for the extra-large model (GPT-NeoX<math id="A7.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{20B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>20B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{20B}}</annotation></semantics></math>).
However, we are unable to verify this on other extra-large models due to the lack of open-sourced models.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A8" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix H </span>Full Zero-shot Evaluation of GPT-3-style Models</h2>

<div id="A8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We includes all zero-shot evaluation results in this section for all GPT-3-style models, inlcuding GPT-NeoX<math id="A8.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{20B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>20B</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{20B}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>

      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
